newsitem.title: USA: Harsh winter in Dakotas may be deadly for calves.
newsitem.headline: Harsh winter in Dakotas may be deadly for calves.

text.p: Cows and heifers that survived four-foot deep snow and weeks of sub-zero temperatures in North Dakota and South Dakota may be so stressed by the ordeal that many may lose their calves this spring.
"We already are getting reports of abortions, mostly in cattle," said Tim Alcorn, a spokesman for South Dakota's Department of Agriculture.
Abundant snow and frigid weather has stressed South Dakota's cattle herd of about 3.9 million head, the eighth largest in the country.
Snowstorms in late December and early January, piled snow nearly four feet deep, preventing ranchers from delivering hay, feed and water to cattle.
The lack of food and water stressed pregnant cows scheduled to calve in February and March.
"I think the heifers that did survive will have a higher abortion rate," said Bob Wilson, an Englewood, Colo. livestock analyst.
Wilson said cattle in South Dakota, North Dakota and northern Nebraska sustained the greatest stress from the cold and snow.
He said talk in the industry has cattle deaths numbering 100,000 to 140,000 head in the Dakotas.
Dale Benson, analyst with Dean Witter, said the impact of South Dakota's calf losses and low breeding rates may cause slightly higher feeder cattle prices late this year and early next year.
Benson estimated feeder cattle prices could be $0.75 to $1.00 per cwt higher than they would have been without the inclement weather.
Cal Sandmeier, a Bowdle, S.D. rancher, said 25- to 30-foot snow drifts made it nearly impossible to get feed to cattle.
He used a huge snowblower attached to a 220-horsepower tractor, but some of his neighbors do not have such equipment.
Sandmeier's nearly 350 cows are to calve in April and so far, just one has aborted, but he said other ranchers unable to deliver feed have reported much higher abortion rates.
"This is strange country. Yesterday (Tuesday) we had 30 to 35 degree weather, today we have 30 to 35 below (zero) wind chill," he said.

Cattle deaths from the cold and snow are expected to be high, but it will be several weeks before losses can be accurately tabulated, said Don Boggs, an extension beef specialist at South Dakota State University.

In addition to higher-than-normal abortion rates this spring, Boggs said the young calves will have a difficult time. Stressed cows often have weak calves and the cows may not provide adequate amounts of milk for the newborns.
"I would expect a little higher death loss in our calf crop than we'd like to see," he said.
Additionally, lingering health stresses from the cold and snow may prevent many cows from being rebred this spring. Boggs said.
